subject: Accounting
title: Operating Expenses
description: A short lesson to help you apply Operating Expenses.

hook.text: Rent, salaries, marketing, utilities—these aren't in the product but still cost money.

buildup.text: Operating expenses cover everything needed to run the business beyond direct production.

discovery.text: Subtract operating expenses from gross profit to get operating income—the real engine metric.

twist.text: A startup burning through cash on marketing may show negative operating income for years.

climax.text: Investors tolerate losses early if they believe operating leverage will eventually flip the numbers.

punchline.text: Revenue minus everything: that's operating income.

quiz.question: What are operating expenses?
options: Costs to run the business beyond production

details.summary: Operating expenses are the costs of running day-to-day business beyond direct production—including sales, marketing, rent, salaries, and R&D. This topic explains what qualifies as an operating expense, how it's reported, and what expense trends reveal about strategy.
details.whyItMatters: Operating expenses consume the gross profit generated by products and services. Managing them effectively is the difference between a company that converts revenue into profit and one that doesn't.
takeaways: Operating expenses include SG&A (selling, general and administrative) and R&D costs
Operating income equals gross profit minus operating expenses—a key measure of business efficiency
Rising operating expenses as a percentage of revenue signal declining operational leverage

faq.question: What counts as an operating expense?
faq.answer: Operating expenses include all costs of running the business beyond production: employee salaries (non-production), rent, marketing, sales commissions, R&D, utilities, insurance, and administrative costs. They exclude COGS, interest, and taxes.

faq.question: What does a rising operating expense ratio indicate?
faq.answer: If operating expenses grow faster than revenue, the company needs more spending to generate each dollar of sales. This declining operating leverage may indicate inefficiency, heavy investment for growth, or loss of pricing power requiring more marketing spend.
